say.text: Last segment. Start with Hesselbach's triangle, the medial gap in the posterior wall of the canal.
Drawn the way exam keys expect, which three edges make it?

choices.label: Deep inguinal ring, rectus edge, Cooper's ligament
Inferior epigastric artery, rectus edge, inguinal ligament
Inferior epigastric artery, superficial ring, inguinal ligament
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The triangle's edges are the inferior epigastric artery laterally, the rectus sheath medially and the inguinal ligament below.
Exam keys use the inguinal ligament as the base. The original description used Cooper's ligament, which is why the older version still tempts.
Tempting: the deep ring is the first landmark you find in the groin, so it feels like part of the hernia's door.
It fails because a ring is a hole in the aponeurosis, not an edge, and Cooper's ligament is the old base rather than the exam key. The edges are the vessel, the rectus and the inguinal ligament.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the picture: the triangle is drawn from the vessel, the rectus and the ligament, not from the ring.

say.text: Tempting: the superficial ring is the opening you see first on examination, so it sounds like a corner of the triangle.
It fails because the superficial ring is a gap in the external oblique aponeurosis, the anterior wall of the canal. The triangle's edges are the vessel, the rectus and the inguinal ligament.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the layers: the superficial ring belongs to the anterior wall, not to the triangle's floor or sides.

say.text: Build it from edges, not holes. One edge is a vessel you can name from the front of the groin, one is a muscle sheath beside the midline, and the floor is a ligament running from the pubic tubercle to the front of the hip.
A registrar says on the ward round: 'The groin hernia most likely to strangulate is the indirect one, since it is the commonest.' Which reply is right?

choices.label: Indirect, because it is the commonest groin hernia
Direct, because its wider sac holds more bowel
Femoral: rarer, but the highest strangulation risk
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Femoral hernia carries the highest strangulation risk of the groin hernias, even though it is rarer than the inguinal types.
Commonness tells you how often a hernia appears, not how often it strangles. This question asks for risk.
Tempting: the indirect hernia is the commonest, so it feels like the answer to every ranking question.
It fails because the stem ranks strangulation risk, and femoral hernia is highest among groin hernias. Commonness does not decide risk.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the question ranks: risk, not frequency. Femoral hernia is highest.

say.text: Tempting: the direct hernia is a big bulge through the wall, so bulk feels like danger.
It fails because a direct sac has a wide neck and classically rarely strangulates. A narrow neck, not a big bulge, is what chokes the bowel.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note this: a wide neck means less constriction, so bulk is not the danger.

say.text: Separate two questions: how often a hernia appears, and what its neck does to the bowel. Then ask which groin type carries the highest risk overall.
Which statement about hernia in women is correct?

choices.label: Inguinal hernia is more common in women than in men
Indirect inguinal hernia is the most common hernia in women
Femoral hernia is the most common hernia in women
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Indirect inguinal hernia is the commonest hernia in women, as it is in men and in children.
Femoral hernia is relatively more common in women than in men, but relatively more common is not the same as the most common.
Tempting: femoral hernia is relatively more common in women, so it sounds like the commonest one.
It fails because relatively more common is not most common. The indirect inguinal hernia still wins in women.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate 'relatively more common' from 'most common'.

say.text: Tempting: inguinal hernia is the commonest hernia overall, so it feels as if it must lean towards women.
It fails because inguinal hernia is far more common in men. The sex difference runs the other way.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the direction: inguinal hernia is far more common in males.

say.text: Two steps: which hernia is the commonest overall, then whether the sex difference changes that answer for women.
Which pairing of patient and operation is correct?

choices.label: A 35-year-old, primary unilateral hernia: laparoscopic TEP by default
A 4-year-old boy, right inguinal hernia: Lichtenstein mesh repair
A 4-year-old boy, right inguinal hernia: herniotomy alone
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A child's defect is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall, so herniotomy alone is the operation.
Herniotomy is excision of the sac, with no repair of the wall.
Tempting: mesh is the modern standard, so it feels like the safe answer for any groin lump.
It fails because the standard adult repair mends a weak wall. A child's posterior wall is normal, so no wall repair is needed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the defect is before the operation. In a child it is the processus, not the wall.

say.text: Tempting: laparoscopy is the newer approach, so it feels like the default for everyone.
It fails because laparoscopy needs a general anaesthetic and a learning curve. For a primary unilateral hernia it is a good option in experienced hands, not the default.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the qualifiers: primary, unilateral and the surgeon's experience decide the route.

say.text: Read the patient first. Age decides whether the posterior wall needs repair at all, and then the qualifiers decide between open and laparoscopic.
A man had an open repair for a primary inguinal hernia. Now he has numbness over the root of the penis and the anterior scrotum. Which nerve is most likely hurt?

choices.label: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, the thigh nerve at risk
Ilioinguinal nerve, the commonest injury in open repair
Femoral nerve, the nerve of the front of the thigh
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The ilioinguinal nerve lies in the field of an open repair, and its loss gives numbness over the root of the penis, the anterior scrotum and the upper medial thigh.
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is the one laparoscopy puts most at risk.
Tempting: the thigh nerve is the famous one in groin surgery, so it feels like the nerve at risk for any repair.
It fails because it is the nerve most at risk in laparoscopic repair. In open repair the ilioinguinal nerve is the one most often injured.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie the nerve to the approach before you name it.

say.text: Tempting: the femoral nerve lies close to the groin, so injury seems likely in any groin dissection.
It fails because the femoral nerve lies in the triangle of pain. It is not the nerve most commonly injured in open repair; the ilioinguinal nerve is.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the nerves by the triangle they run in, not by how close they sit.

say.text: Ask which nerve sits in the open field most often, and whether the numbness fits that nerve or the thigh one.
Which finding in the invagination test points to an indirect hernia?

choices.label: Impulse on the pulp of the little finger, in the invagination test
Impulse on the tip of the little finger, in the invagination test
Swelling returns medial to the finger when the deep ring is held

say.text: Yes. In the invagination test an impulse on the tip of the finger means an indirect hernia, and an impulse on the pulp means a direct one.
With the deep ring held shut, an indirect sac does not return; a direct sac still bulges medial to the finger.
Tempting: tip and pulp are easy to swap when you memorise the finger rules by rote.
It fails because the tip is the sign of an indirect sac and the pulp of a direct one. The pulp is the direct sign, not the indirect one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie each finger part to the sac it detects, not to a memorised order.

say.text: Tempting: you may remember that the occlusion test looks for the swelling to stay away, so a return looks like an indirect sign.
It fails because the finger blocks an indirect sac, which stays away. A direct sac comes through the wall beside the finger and returns medial to it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so work out where the sac comes through before you name the sign.

say.text: Amyand's hernia and de Garengeot's hernia both contain an appendix. Which pairing is right?

choices.label: Amyand's in a femoral sac, de Garengeot's in an inguinal sac
Amyand's in an inguinal sac, de Garengeot's in a femoral sac
Both in inguinal sacs, since both are appendix hernias

say.text: Yes. Amyand's is an appendix in an inguinal sac, and de Garengeot's is an appendix in a femoral sac.
Both are appendix hernias, so the site is the only thing that tells them apart.
Tempting: the two names are close, so the site is easy to flip when you answer quickly.
It fails because Amyand's is the appendix in an inguinal sac and de Garengeot's is the appendix in a femoral sac.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the site: Amyand's inguinal, de Garengeot's femoral.

say.text: Tempting: you learned the appendix eponym once and gave both names the inguinal site.
It fails because de Garengeot's is the femoral one. The site is what separates the two appendix hernias.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that the site is the discriminator, not the organ.

say.text: Which structure forms the medial edge of the triangle of doom?

choices.label: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, the medial edge

say.text: Yes. The vas deferens is the medial edge, and the gonadal vessels are the lateral edge, with the external iliac vessels inside.
This is the vascular triangle, and tacks must stay out of it.
Tempting: the gonadal vessels are the famous landmark, so they feel as if they belong to every edge.
It fails because they form the lateral edge. The vas deferens is the medial edge of the triangle of doom.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the vessels on the lateral side and the duct on the medial side.

say.text: Tempting: nerves are what you dread in groin surgery, so a nerve sounds like a boundary of the dangerous zone.
It fails because the triangle of doom is vascular. The nerves belong to the triangle of pain, on the other side of the gonadal vessels.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate doom, the vessels, from pain, the nerves.

say.text: An older question paper asks for the classic open repair of an inguinal hernia. Which pairing is right, the expected key and current practice?

choices.label: Bassini expected; current practice is still Bassini
Shouldice expected; current practice is Lichtenstein
Bassini expected; current practice is Lichtenstein mesh

say.text: Yes. Older keys expected Bassini, which sutures the conjoint tendon under tension. Current practice is Lichtenstein mesh repair, and Shouldice is the best tissue repair.
Tempting: Bassini is the classic repair, so it feels right whatever the year of the paper.
It fails because the key and current practice differ. Bassini is the older key, and the current open standard is Lichtenstein mesh repair.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so teach both columns: PYQs expected Bassini, and current practice is Lichtenstein.

say.text: Tempting: Shouldice is the best tissue repair, so it feels like the best open answer.
It is partly right, but it is not the expected key for classic open repair, and current practice for mesh is Lichtenstein.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the tissue repair and the mesh standard as two separate answers.

say.text: A surgeon excises a child's hernia sac and leaves the posterior wall alone. Which term fits this operation?
Yes. Herniotomy is excision of the sac, the operation for a child, with nothing added to the wall.
Tempting: the 'rrhaphy' ending sounds like the repair word, so the repair option feels right.
It fails because herniorrhaphy adds repair of the posterior wall with the patient's own tissue. This operation adds nothing.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count what is added to sac excision: nothing for herniotomy.

say.text: Tempting: mesh is the modern picture of any hernia operation, so mesh-sounding words feel right.
It fails because hernioplasty reinforces the wall with a prosthetic mesh. Excision alone is herniotomy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the three terms by what is added: nothing, own tissue, or mesh.

say.text: Three checks settle most hernia answers: where the sac sits against the inferior epigastric vessels, which qualifier the stem uses, and the patient in front of you.

cards.q: Which three edges make Hesselbach's triangle in exam keys?
cards.a: The inferior epigastric artery laterally, the lateral rectus sheath medially and the inguinal ligament below. Cooper's ligament was the original base.

cards.q: In Zieman's test, which finger sits over the superficial ring?
cards.a: The middle finger. An impulse there means a direct hernia.
Indirect inguinal hernia. Femoral hernia is relatively more common in women, but it is not the commonest.

cards.q: Which groin hernia is most likely to strangulate?
cards.a: Femoral hernia. A direct hernia is the classic answer for the one that rarely strangulates.

cards.q: Operation for a child's inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Herniotomy alone, because the defect is a patent processus with a normal posterior wall.

cards.q: Repair for a bilateral or recurrent hernia after open repair?
cards.a: Laparoscopic TEP or TAPP. The open adult standard is Lichtenstein mesh repair.

cards.q: Nerve most at risk in open repair, and in laparoscopic repair?
cards.a: Ilioinguinal nerve in open repair; lateral femoral cutaneous nerve in laparoscopic repair.

cards.q: What lies in the triangle of doom?
cards.a: The external iliac vessels, bounded by the vas deferens medially and the gonadal vessels laterally.
Amyand's: appendix in an inguinal sac. De Garengeot's: appendix in a femoral sac.
